newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria under growing pressure over Kurd slayings.
newsitem.headline: Austria under growing pressure over Kurd slayings.

text.p: Austria came under growing pressure on Wednesday to begin an inquiry into the 1989 shooting of three Kurds in Vienna after the widow of one victim said Iranian intervention had perverted the course of justice.

Less than a week after a German court accused Iran of ordering the slaying in 1992 of four exiled dissidents in Berlin, Austria faces increasing accusations that it bowed to pressure to let the Iranian suspected killers escape.
The three suspected killers were never tried and warrants for their arrest were only issued after they had left the country.
The government is believed to have held two of the men in custody before putting one on a plane back to Tehran and letting the other seek refuge in the Iranian embassy.
Helen Ghassemlou, French widow of the late Kurdish dissident leader Abdul Rahman Ghassemlou, praised the German government and said Austria had shown it was susceptible to external pressure.

"The German government respects the independence of its justice even though it is not easy for them. That is the difference between Austrian and German justice," Ghassemlou told a news briefing in a Vienna cafe.

"If the Austrian government had had enough courage to stand up to the threats it might have stopped subsequent terrorist actions of the Iranian government," she said. However, it was never too late to tell the truth, she added.
Susanne Rasoul Rocken-Schaub, widow of one of the other Kurds, has accused the authorities of turning a blind eye to the killings so as not to jeopardise Austro-Iranian ties.
The opposition Green Party has demanded the case be reopened immediately and a parliamentary inquiry committee set up to establish what really happened.
Chancellor Viktor Klima said on Tuesday a parliamentary inquiry was not necessary and that investigations by an independent judge were already underway.

But Green Party member of Parliament Peter Pilz told reporters his party had assembled new documents and statements from witnesses and would step up pressure on the government for a parliamentary investigation.

"Nothing can be done in terms of the law now. The murderers are out of the country. But we can investigate what happened and show the world that Austria is not willing to be an exercise ground for Iranian terrorists,"

Kenneth Timmerman, a U.S. author and head of a research group which monitors human rights in Iran, alleges that high-level meetings took place between the Austrian and Iranian governments and that Austria deliberately let the killers go out of political expediency.

"I was told by a senior (Austrian) official that it was really very simple. One, it was money, the Austrian government did not want to cut off trade with Iran; and two, they did not want Iranian retaliation on Austrian soil," he told Austrian state radio last week.
All European Union members, except Greece, recalled their envoys to Iran for consultations after the German court ruling. Canada, Australia and New Zealand took similar steps.
Iran has repeatedly denied all involvement in the murders, blaming them on infighting among opposition groups.
